passages.t: The weak and the strong: do not despise, do not judge
passages.happening:
“Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions” (verse 1). One person believes he may eat anything. Another, who is weak, eats only vegetables (verse 2).

“The one who eats everything must not belittle the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him” (verse 3). Who are you to judge someone else's servant? “To his own master he stands or falls” (verse 4).

“One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (verse 5). Both do it to the Lord, and both give thanks to God (verse 6).

None of us lives or dies to himself alone. “So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord” (verse 8). That is why Christ died and rose: to be Lord of the dead and the living (verse 9).

“Why, then, do you judge your brother? Or why do you belittle your brother? For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat” (verse 10). “So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The churches in Rome were divided over food and holy days. Most readers think the tension was mainly between Jewish and Gentile believers. Many Jewish believers went on keeping the food laws of Moses and the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, and the feasts of Israel. Many Gentile believers did not. Jewish families keep these practices to this day, as a way of honouring God, and Paul speaks of them with respect.

Why would someone eat ‘only vegetables’? In a pagan city, meat in the market often came from animals offered in temples, and a Jew could not be sure it had been prepared as the law required. Some therefore avoided meat altogether, as Daniel did in Babylon. Others may have had wider scruples about food offered to idols.

Paul uses two labels: ‘weak’ and ‘strong’. He counts himself among the strong (15:1). But notice that he does not tell the weak to become strong. He tells both sides how to treat each other. Each side had its own temptation. The strong would ‘belittle’, look down on the weak as narrow. The weak would ‘judge’, condemn the strong as careless. Paul forbids both.

His reason is simple. Every believer is the Lord's servant, not yours. God has accepted him. And each person will answer to God, not to his fellow believers.
passages.ot:
The food laws come from the law of Moses. Leviticus 11 lists clean and unclean animals, and says, “be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). The Sabbath is one of the Ten Commandments: “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy” (Exodus 20:8). For faithful Jews these were ways of living as God's holy people among the nations.

Daniel in Babylon “made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food or wine” (Daniel 1:8), and asked, “Let us be given only vegetables to eat and water to drink” (Daniel 1:12).

Verse 11 quotes Isaiah. In Isaiah 45 God says, “Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance” (Isaiah 45:23). Paul's opening words, ‘As surely as I live, says the Lord’, are God's oath, found elsewhere in Isaiah: “As surely as I live” (Isaiah 49:18). In Isaiah the point is that every nation will one day bow to Israel's God. Paul uses it to say that every believer will answer to God, so no believer should sit as judge over another.
passages.hard:
Does ‘each one should be fully convinced in his own mind’ mean that every belief is a private matter? No. Paul is speaking of food and days, things that both sides could do ‘to the Lord’ with thanks. He was not so relaxed about everything. When some taught that Gentiles must keep the law of Moses to be right with God, he opposed them strongly: “if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all” (Galatians 5:2). And at the end of this letter he warns against those who teach what is “contrary to the teaching you have learned” (Romans 16:17).

So Christians have long drawn a line between the gospel itself and matters of conscience on which faithful believers may differ. Some of the church's teachers called the second group ‘things indifferent’. But Christians draw the line in different places. Some draw it at the historic creeds. Others include more: teaching on baptism, worship, or ethics. These notes do not settle where it falls. Paul's test for the matters on the far side of the line is this: can both practices be done to the Lord with thanksgiving? If so, do not despise, and do not judge.
passages.asks: Think of a practice that some believers you know keep and others do not. Ask which side you are on, and which temptation is yours: to belittle or to judge. Then pray for one person on the other side, by name, as the Lord's servant, not yours.

passages.t: ‘Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food’
passages.happening:
“Therefore let us stop judging one another. Instead, make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way” (verse 13).

“I am convinced and fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean” (verse 14). If your eating distresses your brother, you are no longer walking in love. “Do not by your eating destroy your brother, for whom Christ died” (verse 15).

“For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (verse 17). “So then, let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification” (verse 19). All food is clean, but it is wrong to make your eating a stumbling block (verse 20). It is better not to eat meat or drink wine, or do anything that makes your brother stumble (verse 21).

Keep your belief about these things between yourself and God (verse 22). But the one who doubts is condemned if he eats, because he does not eat from faith, “and everything that is not from faith is sin” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Now Paul speaks mostly to the strong. He agrees with them on the facts: ‘nothing is unclean in itself’. The word ‘unclean’ here is the ordinary Jewish word for food that was ritually impure. But he says knowing you are right is not enough. Love asks how your freedom affects someone else.

A ‘stumbling block’ is something that trips a person. Paul means leading a fellow believer to do what his own conscience tells him is wrong, and so to fall away from trust in God.

‘Destroy your brother, for whom Christ died.’ The words are sharp on purpose. Christ died for that person. Will you wound him over a meal?

‘Mutual edification’ means building each other up, as a house is built. The church is a house God is building. Food is too small a thing to tear it down.

Verse 23 is about conscience. If a believer thinks something is wrong and does it anyway, he sins, because he is acting against his faith in God. So no one should be pushed to act against his conscience, even about something that is not wrong in itself.
passages.ot:
The law already forbade placing a stumbling block: “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God” (Leviticus 19:14). Paul turns the picture to conscience.

‘Righteousness, peace, and joy’ are the marks of God's reign in the prophets and psalms. Isaiah's messengers bring news of peace and salvation and say to Zion, “Your God reigns!” (Isaiah 52:7).

Wine is a good gift in Scripture, “wine that gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15). Paul does not say wine is wrong. He says a believer should be ready to give up even a good thing for a brother's sake.
passages.hard:
If ‘nothing is unclean in itself’, did Paul think the food laws were wrong? Readers differ. Many Christians read verse 14 with Jesus' words in Mark, where Mark adds, “Thus all foods are clean” (Mark 7:19), and with Peter's vision, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15). They hold that the food laws do not bind believers in Christ. Others, including some Jewish believers in Jesus today, hold that Jewish believers may rightly keep them as part of their calling as Jews, while Gentiles were never asked to. Both readings agree with Paul's point here: the kingdom is not about food, and neither side may despise or judge the other.

Does this chapter mean that the most easily offended person in a church decides what everyone may do? Many readers say no. The ‘weak’ in Paul's sense is someone whose own conscience could be wounded and led into sin, not someone who simply disapproves. Paul still calls the strong to give way in love where a brother could truly stumble. Churches and believers weigh these cases differently.
passages.asks: Think of a freedom you enjoy that a fellow believer thinks is wrong. Ask whether using it in front of him could lead him to act against his conscience. Ask what you would be willing to give up for his sake, and whether your freedom or your brother matters more to you.
